```{r data}
# ---- Data: read, clean and derive columns --------------------------------------------------------
raw  <- read.csv(params$data, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
n_in <- nrow(raw)
d <- raw[!is.na(raw$arrivals) & raw$arrivals >= 0 & raw$arrivals %% 1 == 0, ]
d <- d[!duplicated(d[c("date", "time_interval")]), ]
d$date <- as.Date(d$date)
d$day  <- c("Sunday", DAYS[1:6])[as.POSIXlt(d$date)$wday + 1]
if (!"day_type" %in% names(d)) d$day_type <- "Regular"
d$day_type[is.na(d$day_type) | d$day_type == ""] <- "Regular"
d <- d[order(d$date, d$time_interval), ]
slots  <- sort(unique(d$time_interval))
K      <- length(slots)
n_days <- length(unique(d$date))
```

```{r estimation}
# ---- Per-slot Poisson estimation, exact (Garwood) CI and overload probability ---------------------
summ <- do.call(rbind, lapply(slots, function(s) {
  x <- d$arrivals[d$time_interval == s]; m <- length(x); S <- sum(x)
  data.frame(slot = s, m = m, total = S, lambda = S / m, var = var(x),
             ci_low = qchisq(ALPHA / 2, 2 * S) / (2 * m), ci_high = qchisq(1 - ALPHA / 2, 2 * S + 2) / (2 * m))
}))
summ$p_over      <- ppois(C, summ$lambda, lower.tail = FALSE)          # P(X > C) = 1 - P(X <= C)
summ$p_over_low  <- ppois(C, summ$ci_low, lower.tail = FALSE)
summ$p_over_high <- ppois(C, summ$ci_high, lower.tail = FALSE)
summ$risk <- ifelse(summ$p_over < LOW, "Low", ifelse(summ$p_over > HIGH, "High", "Medium"))

# ---- Goodness of fit: chi-square with categories merged until E >= 5 (Cochran), and dispersion test ----
gof_test <- function(x, min_exp = 5) {
  n <- length(x); lam <- mean(x)
  kmax <- max(max(x), qpois(1e-12, lam, lower.tail = FALSE)) + 1
  prob <- function(lo, hi) if (is.infinite(hi)) ppois(lo - 1, lam, lower.tail = FALSE) else
    ppois(hi, lam) - ppois(lo - 1, lam)
  singles <- c(lapply(0:(kmax - 1), function(k) c(k, k)), list(c(kmax, Inf)))
  groups <- list(); cur <- NULL
  for (s in singles) {
    cur <- if (is.null(cur)) s else c(cur[1], s[2])
    if (n * prob(cur[1], cur[2]) >= min_exp) { groups[[length(groups) + 1]] <- cur; cur <- NULL }
  }
  if (!is.null(cur)) groups[[length(groups)]][2] <- cur[2]      # leftover right tail joins the last group
  E <- sapply(groups, function(g) n * prob(g[1], g[2]))
  O <- sapply(groups, function(g) sum(x >= g[1] & x <= g[2]))
  chi2 <- sum((O - E)^2 / E); df <- length(groups) - 2
  list(lambda = lam, chi2 = chi2, df = df, p = pchisq(chi2, df, lower.tail = FALSE), k = length(groups))
}
disp_test <- function(x) {
  m <- length(x); D <- (m - 1) * var(x) / mean(x)
  c(index = var(x) / mean(x), D = D, p = min(1, 2 * min(pchisq(D, m - 1), pchisq(D, m - 1, lower.tail = FALSE))))
}
fits <- lapply(slots, function(s) gof_test(d$arrivals[d$time_interval == s]))
summ$gof_p  <- sapply(fits, `[[`, "p")
summ$disp_p <- sapply(slots, function(s) disp_test(d$arrivals[d$time_interval == s])["p"])
rejections  <- sum(summ$gof_p <= ALPHA)
binom_p     <- pbinom(rejections - 1, K, ALPHA, lower.tail = FALSE)   # P(at least this many | all Poisson)

# ---- Least-crowded slot: exact conditional test against the runner-up -----------------------------
ranked <- summ[order(summ$lambda, summ$slot), ]
best <- ranked[1, ]; runner <- ranked[2, ]
quiet_p <- pbinom(best$total, best$total + runner$total, best$m / (best$m + runner$m))

# ---- Capacity planning: smallest C with P(X > C) below a target --------------------------------
required_capacity <- function(lam, target) {
  c <- max(1, qpois(1 - target, lam)); while (ppois(c, lam, lower.tail = FALSE) >= target) c <- c + 1; c }
summ$need20 <- sapply(summ$lambda, required_capacity, target = LOW)
peak <- summ[which.max(summ$lambda), ]; worst <- summ[which.max(summ$p_over), ]
```

```{r model}
# ---- Day-specific forecast: multiple linear regression on log counts ------------------------------
fit_model <- function(dd) {
  dd$slot <- factor(dd$time_interval, levels = sort(unique(dd$time_interval)))
  dd$dayf <- factor(dd$day, levels = DAYS[DAYS %in% dd$day])
  types   <- unique(dd$day_type)
  dd$typef <- factor(dd$day_type, levels = c(intersect("Regular", types), sort(setdiff(types, "Regular"))))
  terms <- c("slot", if (nlevels(dd$dayf) > 1) "dayf", if (nlevels(dd$typef) > 1) "typef")
  f <- lm(as.formula(paste("log(arrivals + 0.5) ~", paste(terms, collapse = " + "))), data = dd)
  smear <- mean(exp(resid(f)))                                    # Duan's smearing factor
  mu <- pmax(exp(fitted(f)) * smear - 0.5, 0.05)
  pearson <- sum((dd$arrivals - mu)^2 / mu)                       # Pearson chi-square, df = n - p
  v <- max((pearson - df.residual(f)) / sum(mu), 0)               # day-to-day variance Var(W)
  list(fit = f, smear = smear, mu = mu, v = v, pearson = pearson, dof = df.residual(f),
       slots = levels(dd$slot), days = levels(dd$dayf), types = levels(dd$typef), data = dd)
}
predict_day <- function(m, weekday, type = "Regular", at = m$slots) {
  nd <- data.frame(slot = factor(at, levels = m$slots), dayf = factor(weekday, levels = m$days),
                   typef = factor(type, levels = m$types))
  setNames(pmax(exp(predict(m$fit, nd)) * m$smear - 0.5, 0.05), at)
}
p_over_mixed <- function(lam, C, v) if (v <= 1e-6) ppois(C, lam, lower.tail = FALSE) else
  pnbinom(C, size = 1 / v, mu = lam, lower.tail = FALSE)          # Poisson-Gamma = negative binomial

M <- fit_model(d)
v <- M$v
disp_p <- pchisq(M$pearson, M$dof, lower.tail = FALSE)
summ$p_mixed <- p_over_mixed(summ$lambda, C, v)
coefs <- summary(M$fit)$coefficients
r2 <- summary(M$fit)$r.squared; adj_r2 <- summary(M$fit)$adj.r.squared

# ---- Day effects on daily totals: ANOVA / Kruskal-Wallis (weekday), Welch t / Mann-Whitney (exam) ---
daily <- aggregate(arrivals ~ date + day + day_type, data = d, FUN = function(x) c(sum = sum(x), n = length(x)))
daily <- data.frame(daily[1:3], total = daily$arrivals[, "sum"], n = daily$arrivals[, "n"])
daily <- daily[daily$n == K, ]
reg_days <- daily[daily$day_type == "Regular", ]
aov_w <- oneway.test(total ~ day, data = reg_days, var.equal = TRUE)
kw_w  <- kruskal.test(total ~ day, data = reg_days)
has_exam <- any(daily$day_type != "Regular")
if (has_exam) {
  t_e <- t.test(daily$total[daily$day_type != "Regular"], reg_days$total, var.equal = FALSE)
  u_e <- wilcox.test(daily$total[daily$day_type != "Regular"], reg_days$total, exact = FALSE)
}

# ---- Peak-time probability by simulation, and P(at least one overload) --------------------------
peak_sim <- function(mu, v, n = 20000, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  W <- if (v > 1e-6) rgamma(n, shape = 1 / v, rate = 1 / v) else rep(1, n)
  X <- matrix(rpois(n * length(mu), outer(W, mu)), n, length(mu))
  pk <- max.col(X + matrix(runif(length(X), 0, 0.5), n), ties.method = "first")
  list(p_peak = setNames(tabulate(pk, length(mu)) / n, names(mu)),
       p_any = mean(rowSums(X > C) > 0), expected = mean(rowSums(X > C)))
}
cases <- data.frame(day = c("Monday", "Friday", "Monday"), type = c("Regular", "Regular", "Exam"))
if (!"Exam" %in% M$types) cases <- cases[1:2, ]
fc <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(cases)), function(i) {
  mu <- predict_day(M, cases$day[i], cases$type[i]); s <- peak_sim(mu, v)
  c(list(mu = mu, p = p_over_mixed(mu, C, v)), s) })
mon <- fc[[1]]
top2 <- names(sort(mon$p_peak, decreasing = TRUE))[1:2]

# ---- Same-day Bayesian update: Gamma prior on the busyness factor W --------------------------------
mu_mon <- mon$mu; k_seen <- 2
obs_seen <- round(mu_mon[1:k_seen] * 1.15)                         # a morning 15% busier than forecast
a <- 1 / max(v, 1e-6)
post_shape <- a + sum(obs_seen); post_rate <- a + sum(mu_mon[1:k_seen])
rest <- mu_mon[-(1:k_seen)]
upd <- data.frame(slot = names(rest), mu = rest, before = p_over_mixed(rest, C, v),
                  after = pnbinom(C, size = post_shape, prob = post_rate / (post_rate + rest), lower.tail = FALSE))
```

```{r backtest}
# ---- Validation: forecast each day from earlier days only (expanding window, first 30 days training) ----
TRAIN <- 30; UPD <- 2
dates <- sort(unique(d$date))
set.seed(7)
rows <- list(); days_out <- list()
for (i in (TRAIN + 1):length(dates)) {
  train <- d[d$date < dates[i], ]; test <- d[d$date == dates[i], ]; test <- test[order(test$time_interval), ]
  m <- fit_model(train)
  if (!test$day[1] %in% m$days) next
  type <- if (test$day_type[1] %in% m$types) test$day_type[1] else "Regular"   # unseen exam type -> regular
  base_all <- tapply(train$arrivals, train$time_interval, mean)
  test <- test[test$time_interval %in% m$slots & test$time_interval %in% names(base_all), ]
  x <- test$arrivals; mu <- predict_day(m, test$day[1], type, test$time_interval)
  base <- as.numeric(base_all[test$time_interval]); vv <- m$v
  cdf <- function(q) if (vv <= 1e-6) ppois(q, mu) else pnbinom(q, size = 1 / vv, mu = mu)
  qf  <- function(p) if (vv <= 1e-6) qpois(p, mu) else qnbinom(p, size = 1 / vv, mu = mu)
  pit <- cdf(x - 1) + runif(length(x)) * (cdf(x) - cdf(x - 1))      # randomised PIT for counts
  p_upd <- rep(NA, length(x)); kk <- min(UPD, length(x) - 1)
  aa <- 1 / max(vv, 1e-6); sh <- aa + sum(x[1:kk]); rt <- aa + sum(mu[1:kk])
  p_upd[-(1:kk)] <- pnbinom(C, size = sh, prob = rt / (rt + mu[-(1:kk)]), lower.tail = FALSE)
  rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
    date = dates[i], actual = x, mu = mu, base = base, p_model = p_over_mixed(mu, C, vv),
    p_base = ppois(C, base, lower.tail = FALSE), p_upd = p_upd, over = as.numeric(x > C),
    covered = as.numeric(x >= qf(0.025) & x <= qf(0.975)), pit = pit)
  days_out[[length(days_out) + 1]] <- data.frame(
    date = dates[i], day = test$day[1], day_type = test$day_type[1],
    mae_model = mean(abs(x - mu)), mae_base = mean(abs(x - base)),
    hit = x[which.max(mu)] == max(x), n_tied = sum(x == max(x)), n_slots = length(x))
}
S <- do.call(rbind, rows); Dd <- do.call(rbind, days_out)

brier <- function(p, o) mean((p - o)^2)
B_model <- brier(S$p_model, S$over); B_base <- brier(S$p_base, S$over)
U <- S[!is.na(S$p_upd), ]
B_upd <- brier(U$p_upd, U$over); B_noupd <- brier(U$p_model, U$over)
ztest <- function(succ, n, p0, alt = "two.sided") {
  z <- (succ / n - p0) / sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n)
  c(phat = succ / n, z = z, p = if (alt == "greater") pnorm(z, lower.tail = FALSE) else 2 * pnorm(-abs(z))) }
cov_t  <- ztest(sum(S$covered), nrow(S), 0.95)
chance <- mean(Dd$n_tied / Dd$n_slots)
hit_t  <- ztest(sum(Dd$hit), nrow(Dd), chance, "greater")
pair_t <- t.test(Dd$mae_base, Dd$mae_model, paired = TRUE, alternative = "greater")
wins <- sum(Dd$mae_base > Dd$mae_model); losses <- sum(Dd$mae_base < Dd$mae_model)
sign_t <- binom.test(wins, wins + losses, 0.5, alternative = "greater")
ks_t   <- ks.test(S$pit, "punif")
pit_counts <- table(cut(S$pit, seq(0, 1, 0.1), include.lowest = TRUE))
chi_t  <- chisq.test(pit_counts)
cor_t  <- cor.test(S$mu, S$actual)
grp <- ifelse(Dd$day_type != "Regular", "Exam days", ifelse(Dd$day == "Friday", "Fridays", "Other regular days"))
mae_grp <- aggregate(cbind(mae_model, mae_base) ~ grp, data = cbind(Dd, grp = grp), FUN = mean)
mae_grp$n <- as.numeric(table(grp)[mae_grp$grp])

reliability <- function(p, o) {
  b <- findInterval(p, c(0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(sort(unique(b)), function(i)
    data.frame(bin = i, forecast = mean(p[b == i]), observed = mean(o[b == i]), n = sum(b == i))))
}

# ---- Dependence checks: consecutive-slot rank correlation, runs test on daily residuals ----------
d$ratio <- d$arrivals / M$mu
wide <- reshape(d[c("date", "time_interval", "ratio")], idvar = "date", timevar = "time_interval",
                direction = "wide")
wide <- wide[, c("date", paste0("ratio.", slots))]
cons <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:(K - 1), function(j) {
  a1 <- wide[[j + 1]]; a2 <- wide[[j + 2]]; ok <- !is.na(a1) & !is.na(a2)
  ct <- suppressWarnings(cor.test(a1[ok], a2[ok], method = "spearman"))
  data.frame(pair = paste(slot_lab(slots[j]), "->", slot_lab(slots[j + 1])), rho = unname(ct$estimate),
             p = ct$p.value) }))
res_day <- aggregate(cbind(arrivals, mu = M$mu) ~ date, data = cbind(d, mu = M$mu), FUN = sum)
sgn <- res_day$arrivals > res_day$mu
n1 <- sum(sgn); n2 <- sum(!sgn); runs <- 1 + sum(sgn[-1] != sgn[-length(sgn)])
runs_mean <- 2 * n1 * n2 / (n1 + n2) + 1
runs_var  <- 2 * n1 * n2 * (2 * n1 * n2 - n1 - n2) / ((n1 + n2)^2 * (n1 + n2 - 1))
runs_z <- (runs - runs_mean) / sqrt(runs_var); runs_p <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(runs_z))
```

# Abstract {-}

University canteens see sharp, short-lived rises in arrivals during the lunch peak. This project asks a practical
question: *what is the probability that student arrivals exceed what the serving counters can handle in a particular
15-minute slot, and when will today's peak occur?* Arrivals in each slot are modelled as Poisson counts; a separate rate
$\lambda_t$ is estimated for every slot with an exact confidence interval, the Poisson assumption is tested slot by slot,
and the overload probability $P(X_t > C)$ is converted into low, medium and high risk labels. The analysis is then
extended to prediction: multiple linear regression gives day-specific rates for each weekday and for exam weeks, a
Poisson–Gamma model allows for day-to-day variation, simulation gives the probability that each slot is the day's peak,
and Bayes' theorem updates the forecast from the first counts of the day. Every forecast is checked on days the model has
not seen. On a reproducible synthetic semester of `r n_days` working days, the riskiest slot is
`r slot_lab(worst$slot)` (P = `r pct(worst$p_over)` at C = `r C`); on a regular Monday the peak falls in
`r paste(sort(slot_lab(top2)), collapse = " or ")` with probability `r pct(sum(mon$p_peak[top2]), 0)`; forecast
intervals cover `r pct(cov_t["phat"])` of unseen counts and the busiest slot is named correctly
`r pct(hit_t["phat"], 0)` of the time against `r pct(chance, 0)` by chance.

# Keywords {-}

Poisson distribution; arrival rate estimation; overload probability; chi-square goodness of fit; multiple linear
regression; negative binomial; Bayes' theorem; hypothesis testing; peak-time forecasting; university canteen.

# Introduction

University canteens experience changing arrival intensity during lunch. When more students arrive in a short interval
than the counters can serve, queues form, the dining area becomes crowded and popular dishes run out. Decisions about
when to eat, how many counters to open and when to stagger breaks are usually taken by intuition rather than from
measured arrival behaviour.

Earlier canteen studies model the whole system: pedestrian movement, window choice and seating [21, 22] or queueing
models that assume Poisson arrivals [5, 11, 25]. These models leave a simple question unanswered: how likely is a given
slot to exceed capacity, and when is the peak? This project answers it with the probability and statistics of the
PAMAT501 course. It focuses on **arrival overload risk, not exact waiting time**.

## Aim

To estimate, for each short time slot of the lunch period, the probability that student arrivals at a university canteen
exceed the serving capacity, and to predict when the day's peak will occur, using the Poisson distribution and
statistical tests that are checked against the data rather than assumed.

## Objectives

1. **Collect and organise arrival data:** arrival counts in fixed 15-minute slots across $m$ working days, validated and
   cleaned.
2. **Estimate time-specific rates:** $\hat\lambda_t$ for every slot with an exact confidence interval, and test whether
   the Poisson model fits.
3. **Calculate the overload probability:** $P(X_t > C)$ for a chosen capacity $C$, with its uncertainty, and label each
   slot low, medium or high risk.
4. **Identify useful time windows:** the least-crowded slot, with a test that it is genuinely quieter, and the capacity
   needed at the peak.
5. **Predict the peak time:** day-specific overload probabilities, the probability that each slot is the peak, and an
   update of the forecast from the day's first counts.
6. **Validate the forecasts:** forecast each day from earlier days only and test the forecasts with hypothesis tests.

# Preliminaries

This section collects the probability and statistics used in the project.

**Poisson distribution.** If students arrive independently at a constant rate during a short slot, the number of arrivals
$X_t$ follows a Poisson distribution:
$$P(X_t = x) = \frac{e^{-\lambda_t}\lambda_t^{x}}{x!},\qquad x = 0, 1, 2, \dots,\qquad E[X_t] = \mathrm{Var}(X_t) = \lambda_t .$$

**Estimation.** For slot $t$ observed on $m$ days, the maximum-likelihood estimate is the sample mean,
$\hat\lambda_t = \sum x_i / m$. Since $S = \sum x_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(m\lambda_t)$, the exact (Garwood) confidence
interval is $\left[\chi^2_{\alpha/2}(2S)/2m,\ \chi^2_{1-\alpha/2}(2S+2)/2m\right]$ [8].

**Overload probability.** With capacity $C$ (threshold $K = C + 1$),
$$P(X_t > C) = P(X_t \ge K) = 1 - \sum_{x=0}^{C}\frac{e^{-\hat\lambda_t}\hat\lambda_t^{x}}{x!}.$$
A slot is labelled *Low* if this is below 20%, *High* above 50% and *Medium* otherwise (project decision rules).

**Gamma, negative binomial and Bayes' theorem.** If a whole day is busier or quieter by a factor
$W \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(1/v, 1/v)$ (mean 1, variance $v$), the theorem of total probability gives
$P(X_t = x) = \int_0^\infty \mathrm{Poisson}(x; w\lambda_t)\, g(w)\, dw$, a negative binomial distribution with mean
$\lambda_t$ and variance $\lambda_t + v\lambda_t^2$ [10]. After observing counts $x_1,\dots,x_k$ with forecasts
$\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k$, Bayes' theorem gives the posterior
$W \mid x \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(a + \sum x_t,\ a + \sum \lambda_t)$ with $a = 1/v$.

**Hypothesis tests.** Table \ref{tab:tests-used} lists the tests [12] and their syllabus modules.

| Test | Used for | Module |
|:---|:---|:---:|
| Chi-square goodness of fit (categories merged to $E \ge 5$ [6]) | Do counts follow Poisson($\hat\lambda$)? | M5 |
| Index of dispersion $D = (m-1)s^2/\bar x \sim \chi^2_{m-1}$ | Is variance equal to the mean? | M5 |
| Exact conditional binomial test [17] | Is the quietest slot really quieter? | M2, M5 |
| $t$-tests on regression coefficients | Do slot, weekday and exam effects matter? | M3, M5 |
| One-way ANOVA, Kruskal–Wallis | Do weekdays differ in daily arrivals? | M5 |
| Welch $t$-test, Mann–Whitney $U$ | Are exam days quieter? | M5 |
| $z$-test of a single proportion | Interval coverage; peak-slot hit rate | M4 |
| Paired $t$-test, sign test | Is the forecast more accurate than the per-slot average? | M5 |
| Kolmogorov–Smirnov, chi-square | Are the forecast distributions calibrated? | M5 |
| Pearson and Spearman correlation | Predicted vs actual; carry-over between slots | M3 |
| Wald–Wolfowitz run test | Do busy days follow busy days? | M5 |

: Statistical tests used in the project \label{tab:tests-used}

# Literature Review

Tang et al. [21] counted arrivals in 5-minute segments at a Beihang University canteen and built a pedestrian-flow model
of the whole meal process; they note that arrivals are Poisson within short periods with a rate that changes every few
minutes, but the arrival rate is an input to their simulation, not a quantity they test or predict. Queueing studies set
serving windows from assumed Poisson arrivals [5, 25]; Jiao et al. [11] simulate one constant rate for the whole lunch.
Brown et al. [3] and Kim and Whitt [13] show that Poisson arrivals must be tested, and that long intervals and pooled
days cause overdispersion; Green et al. [9] and Leemis [14] justify short, piecewise-constant rates; Cameron and Trivedi
[4] give overdispersion tests. Forecasting studies predict arrival rates for call centres and ambulance services and
update them during the day [1, 15, 20, 24]; Ibrahim et al. [10] survey them. Shah et al. [19] forecast campus dining
totals per day, and Variskhanov and Arreeras [23] issue a day-level crowd badge from Wi-Fi data. The Brier score [2] and
a skill score against a reference forecast [16] are standard checks for probability forecasts.

**Research gaps.** (1) No per-slot overload probability for a canteen; (2) the Poisson assumption is built in rather than
tested; (3) no prediction of a specific day's rates or peak time, with or without the day's early counts; (4) no test of
canteen forecasts on unseen days. These are gaps of focus and application, not a claim that Poisson modelling of
arrivals is new.

# Data and Data Reference

**Source and status.** Field data collection at the canteen entrance is in progress. Until it is complete, the analysis
uses a **synthetic prototype dataset**, `data/canteen_arrivals.csv`, generated by the project's `data_generator.py` with a
fixed random seed (42). These values are not observed results; they are used to develop and check the methods, which
apply unchanged to field counts.

**Collection protocol (field data).** Arrivals are counted at the canteen entrance, manually or from permitted video, in
fixed 15-minute slots from 12:30 to 14:30 on $m$ working days, following the observation style of Tang et al. [21].

**How the prototype data were generated.** `r n_days` working days (one 18-week semester) × `r K` slots. Expected
arrivals follow a background of 14 per slot plus a Gaussian lunch rush centred at 13:15; each day gets a Gamma busyness
factor (mean 1, coefficient of variation 5%) and a weekday effect (Friday 6% quieter); weeks 9 and 18 are exam weeks with
demand reduced by 15%; counts are drawn from the resulting Poisson distributions; 0.5% of counts are blanked to exercise
the cleaning step. The analysis below never uses these parameters: it re-estimates everything from the counts.

**Cleaning.** Missing, negative, fractional and duplicate counts are dropped rather than imputed, because imputing the
mean would shrink the variance and bias the dispersion test. Of `r n_in` records, `r n_in - nrow(d)` were missing,
leaving `r nrow(d)` slot observations.

```{r schema}
tab(data.frame(Column = c("date", "day", "day_type", "time_interval", "arrivals", "capacity"),
               Meaning = c("Calendar date of the working day", "Weekday (derived from the date)",
                           "Regular or Exam (optional; Regular if absent)", "15-minute slot, HH:MM-HH:MM",
                           "Number of students who entered in the slot", "Capacity C per slot (optional)")),
    "Dataset variables")
tab(head(raw[c("date", "day", "day_type", "time_interval", "arrivals", "capacity")], 5), "First five records")
```

```{r heatmap, fig.cap = "Every recorded count: days (rows) by slots (columns). The dark band is the lunch rush; paler rows are quieter days such as exam weeks.", fig.height = 3.4}
ggplot(d, aes(x = factor(slot_start(time_interval), levels = slot_start(slots)), y = date, fill = arrivals)) +
  geom_tile() + scale_fill_gradient(low = "#E3F4F4", high = INK, name = "Arrivals") +
  scale_y_date(date_labels = "%d %b", expand = c(0, 0)) + labs(x = "Slot start time", y = NULL) +
  theme_report + theme(legend.position = "right", legend.title = element_text(size = 9))
```

# Main Content: Analysis and Results

All results use capacity $C = `r C`$ per slot and significance level $\alpha = `r ALPHA`$.

## Arrival rate per slot

Arrival rates rise from `r sprintf("%.1f", summ$lambda[1])` at `r slot_lab(slots[1])` to a peak of
`r sprintf("%.1f", peak$lambda)` at `r slot_lab(peak$slot)` and fall to `r sprintf("%.1f", summ$lambda[K])` at
`r slot_lab(slots[K])` (Figure \ref{fig:rates}, Table \ref{tab:slots}).

```{r rates, fig.cap = "Estimated arrival rate per slot with exact 95\\% confidence intervals; the dashed line is the capacity."}
ggplot(summ, aes(x = factor(slot_start(slot), levels = slot_start(slots)), y = lambda)) +
  geom_col(fill = TEAL, width = 0.62) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high), width = 0.2, colour = INK) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = C, linetype = "dashed", colour = RISK_COL["High"]) +
  annotate("text", x = K, y = C + 1.6, label = paste("capacity C =", C), hjust = 1, size = 3,
           colour = RISK_COL["High"]) +
  labs(x = "Slot start time", y = expression(hat(lambda)[t] ~ "(arrivals per 15 min)")) + theme_report
```

## Does the Poisson model fit?

The chi-square goodness-of-fit test rejects the Poisson model in `r rejections` of `r K` slots, against
`r sprintf("%.1f", ALPHA * K)` rejections expected by chance alone (binomial check `r pv(binom_p)`). Figure
\ref{fig:gof} compares the observed counts in the peak slot with the fitted Poisson distribution.

```{r gof, fig.cap = "Observed distribution of daily counts in the peak slot against the fitted Poisson model."}
xp <- d$arrivals[d$time_interval == peak$slot]
kk <- seq(min(xp) - 2, max(xp) + 2)
ggplot() + geom_col(aes(x = kk, y = sapply(kk, function(k) sum(xp == k)), fill = "Observed days"), width = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(x = kk, y = length(xp) * dpois(kk, mean(xp)), colour = "Poisson model"), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(x = kk, y = length(xp) * dpois(kk, mean(xp)), colour = "Poisson model"), size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = SOFT) + scale_colour_manual(values = INK) +
  labs(x = paste("Arrivals in slot", slot_lab(peak$slot)), y = "Number of days") + theme_report
```

```{r slots-table}
tab(data.frame(Slot = slot_lab(summ$slot), lambda = sprintf("%.2f", summ$lambda),
               CI = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", summ$ci_low, summ$ci_high),
               VarMean = sprintf("%.2f", summ$var / summ$lambda), Disp = fmtp(summ$disp_p),
               GOF = fmtp(summ$gof_p), P = sprintf("%.2f", 100 * summ$p_over), Risk = summ$risk),
    "\\label{tab:slots}Per-slot estimates, Poisson checks and overload probability",
    col.names = c("Slot", "$\\hat\\lambda_t$", "95\\% CI", "Var/Mean", "Dispersion $p$", "$\\chi^2$ GOF $p$",
                  "$P(X_t>C)$, \\%", "Risk"), escape = FALSE, align = "lccccccc")
```

## Overload probability and risk

`r sum(summ$risk == "High")` slot(s) are high risk, `r sum(summ$risk == "Medium")` medium and
`r sum(summ$risk == "Low")` low. The riskiest is `r slot_lab(worst$slot)` with $P(X > C)$ = `r pct(worst$p_over)`;
across the confidence interval for $\lambda$ it ranges from `r pct(worst$p_over_low)` to `r pct(worst$p_over_high)`.
Keeping the overload probability below 20% in every slot would need a capacity of `r max(summ$need20)` per slot at the
peak, against `r C` at present.

```{r overload, fig.cap = "Overload probability per slot, coloured by risk level, with the 20\\% and 50\\% thresholds."}
ggplot(summ, aes(x = factor(slot_start(slot), levels = slot_start(slots)), y = 100 * p_over, fill = risk)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.62) + geom_hline(yintercept = c(20, 50), linetype = "dotted", colour = GREY) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = RISK_COL, breaks = c("Low", "Medium", "High")) +
  labs(x = "Slot start time", y = "P(X > C), %") + ylim(0, 100) + theme_report
```

## Least-crowded time

The quietest slot is `r slot_lab(best$slot)` ($\hat\lambda$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", best$lambda)`). Conditional on the
combined total, $S_1 \mid (S_1 + S_2) \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(S_1 + S_2, m_1/(m_1+m_2))$ under $H_0: \lambda_1 = \lambda_2$
[17]; against the runner-up `r slot_lab(runner$slot)` ($\hat\lambda$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", runner$lambda)`) the one-sided
p-value is `r format(quiet_p, digits = 2)`, so it is `r ifelse(quiet_p <= ALPHA, "significantly quieter", "not significantly quieter")`.

## Day-specific forecast by regression

To predict a particular day, log counts are regressed on dummy variables for slot, weekday and day type (reference: first
slot, Monday, regular week): $\ln(x + 0.5) = \beta_0 + \alpha_t + \gamma_d + \delta_e + \varepsilon$. Fitted values are
returned to the count scale with Duan's smearing factor `r sprintf("%.3f", M$smear)` [7]. The model explains
`r pct(r2)` of the variance (adjusted $R^2$ = `r sprintf("%.3f", adj_r2)`; Table \ref{tab:coef}).

```{r coef-table}
cf <- data.frame(Term = sub("^slot", "Slot ", sub("^dayf", "", sub("^typef", "", rownames(coefs)))),
                 Estimate = sprintf("%.4f", coefs[, 1]), SE = sprintf("%.4f", coefs[, 2]),
                 t = sprintf("%.2f", coefs[, 3]), p = fmtp(coefs[, 4]), Multiplier = sprintf("%.3f", exp(coefs[, 1])))
cf$Term <- sub("^Slot (\\d\\d:\\d\\d).*", "Slot \\1", cf$Term); cf$Term[1] <- "Intercept"
cf$Term[cf$Term == "Exam"] <- "Exam week"
tab(cf, "\\label{tab:coef}Regression of $\\ln(x + 0.5)$ on slot, weekday and day type", escape = FALSE,
    col.names = c("Term", "Estimate", "SE", "$t$", "$p$", "$e^{\\hat\\beta}$"), align = "lrrrrr")
```

On daily totals, the weekday effect gives one-way ANOVA F = `r sprintf("%.2f", aov_w$statistic)`
(`r pv(aov_w$p.value)`) and Kruskal–Wallis H = `r sprintf("%.2f", kw_w$statistic)` (`r pv(kw_w$p.value)`).
`r if (has_exam) sprintf("Exam days are quieter: %.1f against %.1f arrivals per lunch (Welch t = %.2f, %s; Mann-Whitney %s).", mean(daily$total[daily$day_type != "Regular"]), mean(reg_days$total), t_e$statistic, pv(t_e$p.value), pv(u_e$p.value)) else ""`

## Peak-time probability

For each kind of day, 20,000 lunch periods are simulated: draw the busyness factor $W$, then
$X_t \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(W\hat\lambda_t)$ for every slot. On a regular Monday the peak is most likely at
`r slot_lab(top2[1])` (`r pct(mon$p_peak[top2[1]], 0)`), and the chance that at least one slot exceeds C is
`r pct(mon$p_any)`, with `r sprintf("%.1f", mon$expected)` overloaded slots expected (Figures \ref{fig:forecast} and
\ref{fig:peak}).

```{r forecast, fig.cap = "Predicted overload probability for three kinds of day (Poisson--Gamma model)."}
fd <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(fc), function(i)
  data.frame(slot = slot_start(names(fc[[i]]$mu)), p = 100 * fc[[i]]$p,
             case = paste0(cases$day[i], ", ", tolower(cases$type[i]), " week"))))
ggplot(fd, aes(x = factor(slot, levels = slot_start(slots)), y = p, colour = case, group = case, shape = case)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(INK, RISK_COL[["Medium"]], TEAL)) +
  labs(x = "Slot start time", y = "Predicted P(X > C), %") + ylim(0, 100) + theme_report
```

```{r peak, fig.cap = "Probability that each slot is the busiest of the day on a regular Monday (20,000 simulated days)."}
pp <- data.frame(slot = factor(slot_start(names(mon$p_peak)), levels = slot_start(slots)), p = 100 * mon$p_peak)
ggplot(pp, aes(x = slot, y = p, fill = p == max(p))) + geom_col(width = 0.62, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(p >= 5, sprintf("%.0f%%", p), "")), vjust = -0.4, size = 3, colour = INK) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = SOFT, `TRUE` = INK)) +
  labs(x = "Slot start time", y = "P(slot is the day's peak), %") + theme_report
```

## Same-day Bayesian update

Suppose the first `r k_seen` slots of a regular Monday bring `r paste(obs_seen, collapse = " and ")` students, about
15% more than forecast. The posterior mean of the busyness factor becomes
`r sprintf("%.3f", post_shape / post_rate)`, and the overload probability of each remaining slot rises (Table
\ref{tab:update}).

```{r update-table}
tab(data.frame(Slot = slot_lab(upd$slot), Forecast = sprintf("%.1f", upd$mu), Before = esc(pct(upd$before)),
               After = esc(pct(upd$after))),
    "\\label{tab:update}Overload probability of the remaining slots before and after observing the first two slots",
    col.names = c("Remaining slot", "Forecast $\\lambda_t$", "$P(X_t>C)$ before", "$P(X_t>C)$ after"),
    escape = FALSE, align = "lccc")
```

## Validation on unseen days

Each day from day `r TRAIN + 1` onward is forecast from all earlier days only: `r nrow(Dd)` days and `r nrow(S)` slot
forecasts. Table \ref{tab:valid} summarises the hypothesis tests; Figures \ref{fig:rel} and \ref{fig:pit} show the
calibration. Updating after the first `r UPD` slots changes the Brier score of the later slots from
`r sprintf("%.4f", B_noupd)` to `r sprintf("%.4f", B_upd)`.

```{r valid-table}
yn <- function(ok) ifelse(ok, "Yes", "No")
tab(data.frame(
  Check = c("95\\% intervals cover actual counts", "Peak slot named correctly", "Lower daily error than baseline",
            "More winning days than baseline", "PIT uniform", "PIT histogram flat"),
  Test = c("$z$, one proportion", "$z$, one proportion", "Paired $t$", "Sign test", "Kolmogorov-Smirnov", "$\\chi^2$ GOF"),
  Statistic = c(sprintf("$z$ = %.2f", cov_t["z"]), sprintf("$z$ = %.2f", hit_t["z"]), sprintf("$t$ = %.2f", pair_t$statistic),
                sprintf("%d wins / %d", wins, wins + losses), sprintf("$D$ = %.3f", ks_t$statistic),
                sprintf("$\\chi^2$ = %.2f", chi_t$statistic)),
  p = fmtp(c(cov_t["p"], hit_t["p"], pair_t$p.value, sign_t$p.value, ks_t$p.value, chi_t$p.value)),
  Result = esc(c(pct(cov_t["phat"]), sprintf("%s vs %s", pct(hit_t["phat"], 0), pct(chance, 0)),
             sprintf("%.2f vs %.2f", mean(Dd$mae_model), mean(Dd$mae_base)), sprintf("%d of %d days", wins, nrow(Dd)),
             ifelse(ks_t$p.value < ALPHA, "not uniform", "uniform"), ifelse(chi_t$p.value < ALPHA, "not flat", "flat"))),
  OK = yn(c(cov_t["p"] >= ALPHA, hit_t["p"] < ALPHA, pair_t$p.value < ALPHA, sign_t$p.value < ALPHA,
            ks_t$p.value >= ALPHA, chi_t$p.value >= ALPHA))),
  "\\label{tab:valid}Hypothesis tests of the one-day-ahead forecasts (model vs baseline: MAE; hit rate vs chance)",
  col.names = c("Check", "Test", "Statistic", "$p$", "Result", "Supports?"), escape = FALSE, align = "lllrlc")
```

```{r rel, fig.cap = "Reliability diagram: forecast overload probability against how often overload actually happened.", fig.height = 3.2, out.width = "70%", fig.width = 5}
rel <- rbind(cbind(reliability(S$p_model, S$over), method = "Regression model"),
             cbind(reliability(S$p_base, S$over), method = "Per-slot average"))
ggplot(rel, aes(x = 100 * forecast, y = 100 * observed, colour = method, shape = method)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dotted", colour = GREY) + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(TEAL, INK)) + coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Forecast P(X > C), %", y = "Observed overload frequency, %") + theme_report
```

```{r pit, fig.cap = "Randomised PIT values of the count forecasts; a flat histogram means a calibrated forecast distribution.", fig.height = 2.8}
ggplot(data.frame(pit = S$pit), aes(x = pit)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1), fill = SOFT, colour = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = nrow(S) / 10, linetype = "dashed", colour = INK) +
  labs(x = "PIT value", y = "Number of slot forecasts") + theme_report
```

**Carry-over and clustering.** Spearman correlations of observed-to-predicted ratios between consecutive slots are
significant for `r sum(cons$p < ALPHA)` of `r nrow(cons)` pairs; the runs test on daily residual signs gives
`r runs` runs against `r sprintf("%.1f", runs_mean)` expected (z = `r sprintf("%.2f", runs_z)`, `r pv(runs_p)`).

# Comparison

## Poisson versus Poisson–Gamma

The Pearson test asks whether whole days vary more than the Poisson model allows once slot, weekday and exam effects are
removed: $\chi^2$ = `r sprintf("%.1f", M$pearson)` on `r M$dof` df, `r pv(disp_p)`, with estimated day-to-day
variance $\hat v$ = `r sprintf("%.4f", v)`. Table \ref{tab:mix} compares the two models' overload probabilities.

```{r mix-table}
tab(data.frame(Slot = slot_lab(summ$slot), Poisson = pct(summ$p_over, 2), Mixed = pct(summ$p_mixed, 2),
               Diff = sprintf("%+.2f", 100 * (summ$p_mixed - summ$p_over))),
    "\\label{tab:mix}Overload probability under the Poisson and Poisson--Gamma models",
    col.names = c("Slot", "Poisson", "Poisson--Gamma", "Difference (points)"), align = "lccc")
```

## Forecast model versus the per-slot average

The per-slot average of past days (the "industry model" [1]) is the natural baseline. Figure \ref{fig:mae} compares the
two day by day, and Table \ref{tab:grp} by kind of day.

```{r mae, fig.cap = "Daily mean absolute error of the regression model against the per-slot average; points below the diagonal are days where the model was more accurate.", fig.height = 3.2, out.width = "70%", fig.width = 5}
ggplot(Dd, aes(x = mae_base, y = mae_model, colour = day_type, shape = day_type)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dotted", colour = GREY) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Exam = RISK_COL[["Medium"]], Regular = TEAL)) + coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Per-slot average: daily MAE", y = "Regression model: daily MAE") + theme_report
```

```{r grp-table}
tab(data.frame(Days = mae_grp$grp, n = mae_grp$n, Model = sprintf("%.2f", mae_grp$mae_model),
               Baseline = sprintf("%.2f", mae_grp$mae_base)),
    "\\label{tab:grp}Mean absolute error by kind of day", col.names = c("Days", "n", "Model MAE", "Baseline MAE"))
```

| | Brier score | Mean absolute error | 95% interval coverage |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Regression + Poisson–Gamma | `r sprintf("%.4f", B_model)` | `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(Dd$mae_model))` | `r pct(cov_t["phat"])` |
| Per-slot average + Poisson | `r sprintf("%.4f", B_base)` | `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(Dd$mae_base))` | — |

: Overall forecast accuracy on unseen days

# Discussion

The per-slot Poisson model fits the slots and turns arrival counts into a direct answer about overcrowding. Testing the
assumption slot by slot, instead of building it in, is what makes the probabilities defensible, and the pooled Pearson
test adds a check that per-slot tests alone can miss. The forecasting results are mixed and are reported as such: the
forecast intervals are close to their nominal coverage, the busiest slot is named far more often than chance, the exam-week
drop is captured, and the same-day update helps; but the gain in point accuracy over the per-slot average is small, in line
with the observation that simple fixed-effect models are hard to beat when day effects are mild [10].

**Limitations.** (i) The data are synthetic; conclusions about the real canteen await field counts. (ii) The model
estimates arrival risk, not queue length, which also depends on service rates and counters. (iii) The rate is assumed
constant within a slot and arrivals independent, although friends often arrive together. (iv) The regression scales a
whole day up or down and cannot move the peak to another slot on special days. (v) Capacity and risk thresholds are
project decisions that must be justified for a specific canteen.

# Conclusion

This project estimated the probability that canteen arrivals exceed capacity in each 15-minute slot using a Poisson
model that was checked slot by slot, and extended it to predict a specific day's risk and peak time. On the prototype
semester it identified a high-risk window around `r paste(sort(slot_lab(top2)), collapse = " and ")`, a significantly
quieter time at `r slot_lab(best$slot)`, the capacity needed at the peak (`r max(summ$need20)` per slot for a 20%
target), and a measurable benefit from updating the forecast with the day's first counts. Future work will replace the
synthetic semester with field counts, add service times for an M/M/c queueing model, model group arrivals, and run the
same-day update automatically from turnstile or camera counts.
